newsitem.title: LEBANON: Banque Audi proposes VAT for Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Banque Audi proposes VAT for Lebanon.

text.p: Banque Audi said Lebanon's chronic budget deficit was due to revenue shortfall rather than overspending and suggested that introduction of Value Added Tax (VAT) would solve the problem.

The bank said in its economic report for the third quarter issued on Tuesday that the deficit of revenue to expenditures for the first nine months of 1996 was 50.2 percent compared with a target for the full year of 37.6 percent.

"The problem is mainly due to revenue as opposed to spending, because even though the volume of spending corresponds to its budgetary forecasts, that of revenues (reaches) only 81 percent of its target," the report said.
Banque Audi is one of Lebanon's leading commercial banks and the reports prepared by its economic analysis unit are well regarded in financial and business circles.

It estimated that one-third of the revenue shortfall was due to Israel's 17-day blitz on Lebanon in April and the rest to the inconsistency of tax collection and the requirements of economic recovery and reconstruction.
"Actually, the objective of the 1996 budget improvement, aiming for a 37 percent deficit, is totally unrealistic," Banque Audi said.
With a 15 percent ratio of revenues to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) 19 percent real economic growth would have been required to meet the target, it said.
However, with a 20 percent ratio of revenue to GDP real growth of four percent would be sufficient to generate the needed revenues, it added.
"The abolition of the total annual deficit requires that a 15 percent VAT be levied on household spending," the report said.
"Selective, it would encompass complementary and not essential products. Progressive, it would reach five percent for low to middle income households and 20 percent for upper income revenues."
